title: A few tricks I've been using
author: max13007
selftext:
* Add a bug report button in your game that can be used to instantly screenshot and log all relevant game data, let you save a note... save it to a folder in your Agent's scope and tell it to review bugs. (I'm a big fan of this one since it lets me focus on staying in the game I'm developing and stay focused on playtesting.)

* Build tools, dont just have it "build the game." Map-making tools, asset importers that are tailored to your workflow, really anything you need. I built a map editor that basically looks and functions exactly like Planet Coaster's build interface because that's what I was comfortable using, and it's been fantastic to jump in and just *know* how to use your own tool. 
* Traditional game dev terms and techniques are very important to know. They can help direct your agent in novel directions. Be sure to keep watching and learning as much as you can from traditional game development.
* "X-Factor Markers" - this one is a little obtuse, but I have an event marker I can set down that basically just opens a text window and allows me to leave a message describing what it is I want in any given scenario. Later on, I have Claude do a pass on X-Factors, and it can build them out. Again, just another way to keep myself focused on playtesting the game itself and staying "in the zone" rather than knee-jerk fixing every little issue as soon as it pops up. 


There's lots more stuff I'm learning and focusing on. I really feel like knowing my game in and out is even more important than ever, now that I have the programming being handled by an agent. I find it really interesting how different everyone's approach to this is, so feel free to share your interesting tips and tricks below.

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body:
Going into my game and just stream of consciousness telling my agent what changes to make is really accelerating my creation process.  It's only when I run into things the AI can't do well yet that things slow down.

I love your idea of developing tools to interact with your agent from within your game.  Great idea.  You also inspired me to put a feedback button on my game for play testers and early adopters.

comments.author: Qinistral
comments.body: Tell me more about the x-factor markers. How is it different than the bug report button? How does claude use them? Do they also contain all the game data or?

replies.author: max13007
replies.body:
They are functionally very similar to the bug reports in that they're both basically something you leave in-game as a "message" for Claude during later reviews. The main difference is largely scope and what remains in-game for me. 

The X Factors stick around as a reminder of the event. For example: I'm designing a racing game, I set up a series of torches along a road, and left an X-Factor marker towards the front of the chamber saying "I'd like all of the torches in this area to light in sequence as a car drives by." - then later Claude can see the note, confirm details and build. But the key is I was able to just keep map-making after dropping the X-Factor marker, staying "in the zone". Plus it's just kinda fun. 

The bug reports were born of the same idea, but with a utilitarian edge. Grab a screenshot and gamedata, debug logs at this state, etc... and I also have Claude automatically delete the bug reports afterwards so they don't pile up (the git tracks fixed bugs so they dont resurface.)

comments.author: CaptainAra
comments.body: I used Claude Code to dumb down Blender for me 😅 I had it reduce the interface to a dozen functions I need to build a scene. Claude created a toddler Version with big ass buttons for me and I love it! 😂

replies.author: _-kman-_
replies.body: Any chance of pushing this to a public github somewhere? :)

replies.author: CaptainAra
replies.body:
Not really, since it's specifically built for my exact use case (down to some obscure names of the buttons and some weird functions that I needed). But it's easy to set up yourself! Just ask Claude Code to make a stripped down, simplified beginner-friendly UI for you. You can tell it up front which functions you want to have, whether you want to have the original version of that or a button that only does certain things with that function without showing the rest. You can add, remove and change that just by telling Claude what you need. 

I stumbled upon that by accident. Never used Blender before and was hit with so many things I didn't understand. Couldn't follow Claude's tips how to model a certain thing I needed and whined about it... It asked me what exactly Was overwhelming for me and then just built me a toddler version without even asking 😅

comments.author: DivineMage1
comments.body:
Point #2 of this is so critical - not only do the tools make it easy to change things about your game, it forces you to architect the game in a scalable way (otherwise the tool doesn't work) - I've built a bunch for my workflows.

On #3 - what term or algorithm or strategy has been the most useful that you've learned recently?

replies.author: max13007
replies.body:
> On #3 - what term or algorithm or strategy has been the most useful that you've learned recently? 

The simplest one is knowing what Z-Fighting is haha - it's little things that you learn passively in traditional game dev, but if you're uninitiated, may take a while to try and describe. 

Another more specific example recently involved explaining specific PS1 rendering techniques I wanted to emulate (vertex jittering and dithering in particular) while working on my PS1/PS2-style racing game. 

There have been other instances for sure. I really enjoy watching game development blogs, so now I've been trying to glean techniques I can use.

replies.author: DivineMage1
replies.body: Thx - that's interesting - I'm familiar with the effect of Z-fighting but I didn't know the name.

comments.author: ScallionZestyclose16
comments.body:
I have a command for cursor ”csv-analyze”.
Combined with a menu command for exporting the analysis profiler to csv.

So I can run the game with analysis enabled and then ask cursor what currently eats performance.

It helps a lot after building new features :)
